items.subject: Hotel-Dieu
items.correct_fact: The two Hôtel-Dieu (Paris) beats claiming the hospital was "founded in the 12th century" are WRONG. The hospital is traditionally said to have been founded c. 651 AD by Saint Landry (28th Bishop of Paris), and the earliest OFFICIAL documented record of it is a charter of the year 829 — over three centuries before the 12th century. The 12th-century milestones the beats conflate with "founding" are (a) the 1157 letters patent that first record the name "Hôtel-Dieu-Saint-Christophe" and (b) Bishop Maurice de Sully's 1165 reconstruction of the buildings (old buildings razed 1195, new ones finished 1255) — both of which post-date documented proof of the institution's existence (829). The corpus is also internally contradictory: a separate beat correctly states "Founded in 651," which directly conflicts with the two "12th century" beats. Resolution: keep the "Founded in 651" beat (correct); correct the two "founded in the 12th century" beats to the 651-traditional / 829-first-documented founding. Note the "19th-century hospital, Hôtel-Dieu" beat is NOT in conflict and should be kept as-is: it correctly describes the CURRENT building, which was entirely rebuilt 1867–1878 on the north side of the Notre-Dame parvis during Haussmann's renovation — the medieval institution long predates the 19th century even though its present building does not.

items.subject: Hotel-Dieu
items.correct_fact: The Hôtel-Dieu de Paris was, by tradition, founded by Saint Landry (Landericus), 28th Bishop of Paris, around 650–651 AD (earliest verified records of a care institution on the site date to 829). Maurice de Sully, the 12th-century Bishop of Paris (r. 1160–1196, famous for beginning Notre-Dame), did NOT found the hospital: in 1165 he undertook the RECONSTRUCTION of the already-existing hospital (old buildings demolished 1195, new construction completed 1255) — a distinct event from the founding. Therefore the two beats crediting "Maurice de Sully" as founder in the 12th century are factually wrong (they conflate his rebuilding with the founding), while the beat crediting "Bishop Saint-Landry" (founded 651) states the historically correct, source-supported attribution.

items.subject: Hotel-Dieu
items.correct_fact: Beds at the Hôtel-Dieu normally held two to three patients each (arranged heel-to-head). The "up to five patients per bed" figure is uncorroborated and single-sourced to Thirza Vallois (her book "Around and About Paris" and her own bonjourparis.com post — same author, not two independent sources). Two genuinely independent authoritative sources give normal capacity as 2–3: the 1913 medical-journal history "The Curious History of L'Hôtel-Dieu de Paris" ("capable of holding normally...three persons") and Charles Coury's definitive academic history via Wikipedia ("meant to hold 2 or 3 patients each"). The corpus internally contradicts itself — one beat says "five," another says "three per bed," and the "three" beat is the one the independent sources support. During extreme crisis periods (famine/plague/Fronde, 15th–17th c.) overcrowding reached as many as 12–14 patients per bed, but that is a distinct extreme-crisis figure, not the baseline the "five" beats assert.

items.subject: Pont au Double
items.correct_fact: The Pont au Double (built 1626) connected the Hôtel-Dieu on the Île de la Cité to its Left Bank annex (the salle Saint-Charles, built 1606) — this "connected the Hotel-Dieu to the Left Bank" clause is CORRECT and should be kept. However, the Pont au Double did NOT feature an enclosed glass gallery for patients to promenade; its superstructure was ward rooms — two stacked salles, the salle Saint-Cosme (also called du Rosaire) — plus a pedestrian passage. The enclosed glazed gallery / promenoir vitré where recovering patients could promenade belonged to the physically adjacent Pont Saint-Charles (situated between the Pont au Double and the Petit-Pont; covered by a "galerie vitrée sur toute sa longueur pour le bien-être des malades," demolished 1854). The corpus's "featured an enclosed glass gallery where recovering patients could promenade" is a bridge-conflation error: the fact is real but describes the neighboring Pont Saint-Charles, not the Pont au Double.

items.subject: Île de la Cité
items.correct_fact: The corpus claim "In the 3rd century AD, the Roman Emperor Julian established his seat on the island" is a century-level (~100-year) date error. Julian (Julian the Apostate) came to Gaul as Caesar in 355 AD; the Palace on the western tip of the Île de la Cité became his military residence in 357 AD; and his troops proclaimed him Augustus at Lutetia (Paris) in February/March 360 AD. His seat/residence on the island therefore belongs to the 4th century AD, not the 3rd century AD. The correct statement is roughly: "In the 4th century AD (c. 357–360), the future Roman Emperor Julian established his residence at Lutetia (the western tip of the island)." The other seven listed values (Parisii settlement c. 3rd century BC/~300 BC, Roman conquest 52 BC, Merovingian royal residence in the 6th century, 14th-century overcrowding driving the kings away, and mid-19th-century cholera/Haussmann demolition) are compatible, describe distinct events, and are independently corroborated — only the Julian-century claim is a genuine factual error.

items.subject: Robert Desnos
items.correct_fact: Robert Desnos — French Surrealist poet and member of the French Resistance, arrested by the Gestapo (Feb 1944) and deported, ultimately to the Theresienstadt (Terezín) camp — died of typhoid at Theresienstadt on 8 June 1945, roughly ONE MONTH AFTER the camp was liberated (8 May 1945, when the Red Army and Czech partisans entered the camp). The corpus framing "died at Theresienstadt just weeks before liberation" inverts the true sequence: he died AFTER liberation, not before. The "poet," "active in the Resistance," "was himself a deportee," and "died at Theresienstadt" attributes are all correct; only the before/after-liberation framing is wrong.

items.subject: Memorial des Martyrs de la Deportation
items.correct_fact: The Mémorial des Martyrs de la Déportation is dedicated to exactly 200,000 people (men, women, and children) deported from France (Vichy France) to the Nazi concentration/death camps during WWII — not "more than 200,000." The crypt holds 200,000 illuminated glass crystals, one for each deportee, so the "200,000 crystals" figure is consistent with (not contradictory to) the deportee count. The official Base Mérimée inscription describes them as "200 000 ... déportés depuis la France ... exterminés dans les camps nazis" (deported from France, exterminated in the Nazi camps), which supports the "died in Nazi concentration camps" framing. The only genuinely contradicted corpus claim is the beat that says "the MORE THAN two hundred thousand people" — the canonical, symbolic dedication figure is exactly 200,000.

items.subject: Conciergerie
items.correct_fact: The Palais de la Cité (later the Conciergerie), on the Île de la Cité, was the permanent royal residence of the French kings from the late 12th century until 1364, when Charles V relocated the court to the Louvre and the Hôtel Saint-Pol. But the Louvre had ALREADY been built as a fortress by Philip II Augustus (ordered 1190, keep built ~1200, completed 1202) — roughly 160 years before it first became a royal residence in 1364. So the Conciergerie was the royal palace before the Louvre became a royal RESIDENCE, not before the Louvre was BUILT: the Louvre already stood as a structure throughout the Conciergerie's entire tenure as the royal palace. The corpus claim's chronology ("before the Louvre was built") is therefore false — the Louvre fortress was built (1202) while the Conciergerie was still the royal palace (until 1364).

items.subject: Tour Bonbec
items.correct_fact: The Tour Bonbec at the Conciergerie takes its name from the French "bon bec," which literally means "good beak" and idiomatically "good talker" / one who "speaks easily/readily" (avoir bon bec = parler facilement). It is a grim reference to the tower's use as the Conciergerie's torture chamber, where prisoners were made to "talk"/confess readily under torture. Accurate renderings are "Good Talker Tower" / "Good Beak Tower" / "Good Word Tower." "Big Mouth Tower" is a mistranslation — it renders the adjective "bon" (good) as "big" and carries a pejorative "blabbermouth" connotation absent from the actual meaning; no historical, official, or tourism source translates it that way.

sources.quote: La Tour Bonbec est l'endroit où on torture les prisonniers pour les faire parler. Avoir bon bec veut dire parler facilement

items.subject: Philippe-Auguste
items.correct_fact: In 1182 Philippe-Auguste did confiscate Jewish property (the beat's core is true), but two elements of the compound claim are inaccurate. (1) SCOPE: the 1182 edict expelled Jews from the royal demesne — the crown's directly-held lands, essentially the Île-de-France — not "France" as a whole. In 1182 the Kingdom of France was a patchwork of largely autonomous fiefs (Plantagenet Normandy/Anjou/Aquitaine, Champagne, Flanders, Burgundy, Toulouse), where Jews continued to live outside royal control. Academic sources are explicit: Bradbury says "royal demesne," and the Jewish Encyclopedia says "royal domains of France (and not the whole kingdom)." (The looser popular phrasing "from the kingdom" also appears, e.g. the mahj museum, so "from France" is a common simplification rather than an outright fabrication.) (2) LES HALLES: the market already existed at the Champeaux site from Louis VI's reign (c.1110); the actual Jewish connection was that confiscated Jewish houses in Paris were demolished to clear the building SITE, and Philippe-Auguste separately purchased the Saint-Lazare fair (1181-83) and erected two covered halls there in 1183 — a land/site and construction transaction. No source supports the beat's assertion that confiscation "proceeds partly financed" the market; that mechanism is mischaracterized.

sources.quote: Philip expelled them from the royal demesne in July 1182 ... had Jewish houses in Paris demolished to make way for the Les Halles market.
In July they were compelled to leave the royal domains of France (and not the whole kingdom) ... The goods confiscated by the king were at once converted into cash.

1181-1183 : Philippe-Auguste achète la foire Saint-Ladre ou Saint-Lazare ... et la transfère à l'emplacement même des futures Halles ... En 1183, deux bâtiments couverts sont élevés pour accueillir le nouveau marché.

items.subject: Conciergerie
items.note: The two beats are not actually testing the same proposition, but one of them is an unresolvable superlative, so the pair cannot be auto-resolved either way. (1) "Paris's oldest prison" is a bare superlative ranking claim (oldest) — per policy this must never be auto-resolved regardless of how many secondary/tourism sources repeat it. (2) "One memoirist called the Conciergerie 'the most lucrative furnished lodgings in Paris'" is a reported-quote/attribution claim, not the corpus asserting an objective ranking itself. This part is well-attested: Honoré Riouffe (1764-1813) was a real detainee held at the Conciergerie during the Terror (arrested Oct 1793, ~14 months' detention) who wrote a memoir of his imprisonment ("Mémoires d'un détenu, pour servir à l'histoire de la tyrannie de Robespierre," 1795; English translation "Revolutionary Justice Displayed," 1796) — confirmed independently via the Bibliothèque nationale de France (Gallica) and Newberry Library catalogs. Wikipedia's exact quote is sourced directly to that 1796 English edition, and the underlying substance (wealthy prisoners paying escalating fees for furnished cells — the "pistole" system) is independently corroborated by the Conciergerie's official operator, Centre des monuments nationaux. However, since no second fully-independent source reproduces the EXACT phrase (all other web hits are verbatim Wikipedia mirrors), and the paired claim under review is a bona-fide superlative ("oldest"), policy requires leaving the pair unresolved rather than picking a winner.

items.subject: Hotel-Dieu
items.note: Not resolved by policy. All four contested statements are variants of a superlative/absolute claim about Hôtel-Dieu de Paris (either "oldest hospital in Paris," "oldest PUBLIC hospital in Paris," or "the only hospital serving the city"). Widely repeated tertiary sources (English and French Wikipedia) describe Hôtel-Dieu as "the oldest in France and possibly the oldest continuously operating hospital in the world" (tradition: founded c. 651 by Bishop Saint Landry; first documented structure 829) and as having been "the only hospital in the city until the beginning of the 17th century" (French Wikipedia: "jusqu'à la Renaissance"). These are consistent with each other in substance, but per policy, superlative claims (oldest/first/only) are never auto-resolved even when sources agree, and "oldest hospital" vs. "oldest PUBLIC hospital" are distinct propositions (the qualifier "public" implicitly concedes there may have been older non-public/religious hospital-like institutions), which further argues against collapsing them into one resolved fact.

items.subject: Île de la Cité
items.note: Île de la Cité is traditionally identified as the site of the Parisii's Gallic settlement (the "oppidum" of Lutetia, conventionally dated to c. 250-3rd century BC) and is the historic core of Paris. However, the specific claim that it was "the first part of Paris to be settled" / "the original settlement of the Parisii" is a genuinely disputed superlative, not a settled fact: (a) no pre-Roman (Gallic-era) archaeological remains have been confirmed on Île de la Cité itself — the earliest confirmed traces there date to the 1st century AD (Gallo-Roman); (b) INRAP excavations (1994-2005) uncovered a major Gallic settlement at Nanterre, and contemporary French historians/archaeologists now consider it "more probable" that the Parisii's principal settlement was off the island (Nanterre, or a since-vanished island near the mouth of the Bièvre) rather than on Île de la Cité; and (c) even setting the Parisii question aside, Neolithic human traces (c. 4500 BC) found elsewhere within modern Paris (e.g. Bercy) predate the Iron-Age Parisii settlement by millennia, undermining a literal "first part of Paris settled" claim. Per policy, this first/original-settlement superlative should not be auto-resolved in either beat's favor.

beats.quoted_span: the first part of Paris to be settled
is the original settlement of the Parisii, a Celtic tribe

items.subject: Pilier des Nautes
items.note: Both beats assert the same superlative claim about the Pilier des Nautes (Pillar of the Boatmen): that it is the oldest sculpted monument found in Paris/the capital. The wording difference ("in the capital" vs. "found in the capital") is cosmetic paraphrase drift, not a substantive factual contradiction — both encode the identical superlative rank-claim. The primary source itself (Thirza Vallois, "Around and About Paris," chunk-09-4th-arr-arsenal.txt) uses the "found in the capital" phrasing verbatim, and multiple independent reference sources (Wikipedia EN/FR, French Ministry of Culture, a dedicated Pilier des Nautes reference site) corroborate the general claim that this Gallo-Roman pillar (dedicated to Jupiter by the Nautae Parisiaci corporation, inscribed to the reign of Tiberius, excavated in 1711 under Notre-Dame's chancel, now at Musée de Cluny) is widely regarded as the oldest (precisely-dated/sculpted) monument in Paris/Lutèce. However, per mandatory policy this is a SUPERLATIVE claim ("oldest") and must NOT be auto-resolved regardless of how strong the corroborating evidence is — it requires human review/decision, not an automated flip of either beat.

items.subject: Notre-Dame Cathedral
items.note: The two beats are not actually describing the same fact-slot, and one of them is an unresolvable superlative, so the "contradiction" cannot be auto-resolved. What IS solidly verified: Notre-Dame's construction began in 1163 under Bishop Maurice de Sully, and the cathedral marked its 850th anniversary with a year-long celebration starting 12 December 2012 through 2013, including new bells cast in 2012 and inscribed "à l'occasion du grand jubilé du 850e anniversaire de la cathédrale (1163–2013)." That beat (dbsync paris_notre_dame_cathedral_music_heritage_wikipedia_bells_recast_2013) is correct and non-superlative. The other beat's claim that Notre-Dame "was the birthplace of polyphonic music in Europe" is a superlative/origin claim and must not be auto-resolved per policy — and independent evidence actually cuts against a literal reading of it: written polyphony in Europe is documented centuries before the Notre-Dame school (Musica enchiriadis/Scolica enchiriadis, c. 900; the Winchester Troper, c. 1000), whereas the Notre-Dame school (Léonin, Pérotin) dates only to c. 1160-1250. Notre-Dame is more accurately the birthplace/center of a specific *style* — measured, rhythmically-notated polyphony (the Magnus Liber Organi / Ars Antiqua) — not of polyphony in Europe overall. Per the fact-check policy this superlative claim is flagged unresolved rather than corrected.

items.subject: Pont Neuf
items.note:
Do not auto-resolve. All four flagged values are superlative claims ("oldest," "first") about Pont Neuf, which per pipeline policy (guardrail: "Never auto-resolve: ... superlatives") must be routed to human review, not auto-corrected — regardless of how the web evidence leans.

For context (not a resolution): "Pont Neuf is the oldest standing bridge in Paris" (asserted identically by both beats, so those two are not actually in conflict with each other) and "Pont Neuf was the first stone bridge in Paris built without houses" are the standard, widely-repeated compound claim in tourism/encyclopedic sources. However, the pipeline decomposed that compound source sentence ("was the first to be built of stone, and to be free of houses") into two independent superlative propositions, and the standalone claim "[Pont Neuf] was the first [bridge in Paris] to be built of stone" (with no qualifier about "without houses" or "across the full Seine") is contradicted by earlier stone bridges in Paris: Petit Pont was rebuilt in stone in 1175, and Pont Notre-Dame was rebuilt in stone by 1507 — both a century-plus before Pont Neuf's 1607 completion. So if this fourth value is read as a bare "first stone bridge in Paris, period" claim, it looks wrong; if read as shorthand for "first stone bridge in Paris built without houses" (the actual well-attested claim), it's fine. That ambiguity is itself a reason a human should adjudicate the exact proposition rather than the pipeline auto-picking a value.

and to be free of houses

items.subject: Tour de l'Horloge clock mechanism
items.note: The non-superlative core of the claim is well-corroborated: Henri de Vic, a clockmaker from Lorraine/Germany, was commissioned by King Charles V (r. 1364–1380) around 1370 to build the clock mechanism for the Tour de l'Horloge at the Conciergerie/Palais de la Cité, which went into service in 1371 — so "built_by = Henri de Vic, during the reign of Charles V" checks out against two genuinely independent sources beyond Wikipedia (tfp-france.org and viewfromtheback.com), plus both EN and FR Wikipedia. However, the beat's second assertion — "the first public clock in Paris" — is a superlative ("first"/"oldest") that policy forbids auto-resolving. Sources are also inconsistent on it: viewfromtheback.com calls it "the oldest (and first) public clock in Paris," while tfp-france.org only claims "la plus ancienne horloge de Paris" (the oldest clock in Paris) without asserting it was the first PUBLIC one specifically — a subtly different and unverified claim. Per policy this superlative portion must be flagged for human review rather than confirmed or corrected; the builder/date attribution itself does not need correction.
